cards.front: Organ holding at steady state: number of lymphocytes an organ holds = {{c1::number entering per hour × average time each one stays}}.
cards.back: The stay is set by the way out, not the way in.
cards.quote: the number of lymphocytes an organ holds = the number entering per hour × the average time each one stays

cards.front: Under what conditions does the rule 'cells held = entry per hour × average stay' hold for lymphoid organs?
cards.back: Naive lymphocytes at steady state (entry equals exit), with no cell division or death. It is false in the first hours after something changes.
cards.quote: Naive lymphocytes at steady state, with no cell division or death; it is false in the first hours after something changes.

cards.front: In humans and mice, B cells develop in the {{c1::bone marrow}}, and T cells mature in the thymus from marrow-derived precursors.
cards.back: Bone marrow and thymus are the primary lymphoid organs.
cards.quote: In humans and mice, B cells develop in the bone marrow from blood-forming stem cells (stem cells), and T cells mature in the thymus from marrow-derived precursors.
cards.section: Lymphocytes go around a loop, not out of a factory

cards.front: Name the secondary lymphoid organs and what happens in them.
cards.back: Lymph nodes, the spleen, and mucosal tissue such as tonsils and Peyer's patches. They host mature lymphocytes and are where those cells meet antigen.
cards.quote: The secondary lymphoid organs (lymph nodes, the spleen, and mucosal tissue such as the tonsils and the Peyer's patches of the gut wall) host mature lymphocytes
cards.section: Lymphocytes go around a loop, not out of a factory

cards.front: Gowans drained a rat's thoracic duct through a chronic cannula for days, and lymphocyte output fell progressively. Which hypothesis did the fall support, and why?
cards.back: That the same cells go around a loop. If nodes made the cells continuously, output should have held roughly steady; removing recirculating cells instead empties the loop.
cards.quote: If the same cells were going around, removing them should empty the loop.
cards.section: Lymphocytes go around a loop, not out of a factory

cards.front: A rat's thoracic duct lymphocytes are collected and then returned into a vein. Predict duct output if nodes are a factory versus a recirculation loop. What was observed?
cards.back: Factory: output stays low, since cells in blood cannot re-enter production. Loop: output refills. Output recovered and returned cells appeared in duct lymph, so the cells recirculate.
cards.quote: Output recovered, and the returned cells were later found in duct lymph.
cards.section: Lymphocytes go around a loop, not out of a factory

cards.front: What is a high endothelial venule (HEV), and what did Gowans conclude it does?
cards.back: A small venule lined by plump, almost cuboidal endothelial cells. It is the site of large-scale lymphocyte migration from blood into secondary lymphoid organs.
cards.quote: small venules lined by plump, almost cuboidal endothelial cells instead of flat ones
cards.section: Lymphocytes go around a loop, not out of a factory

cards.front: Why do naive lymphocytes tour secondary lymphoid organs instead of staying put?
cards.back: Only about one naive T cell in 10^5 to 10^6 recognises a given antigen, so antigen must be brought to places all of them pass through.
cards.quote: so the antigen has to be brought to a place they all pass through.
cards.section: A node samples lymph and blood; the spleen samples blood alone

cards.front: What does the phenotype of CCR7-deficient mice show about how antigen reaches a lymph node?
cards.back: Their activated skin dendritic cells fail to reach the nodes, so dendritic cell travel in afferent lymph to the T-cell zone needs CCR7.
cards.quote: in CCR7-deficient mice, activated skin dendritic cells fail to reach the nodes
cards.section: A node samples lymph and blood; the spleen samples blood alone

cards.front: A lymph node is like a hotel. What are its two entrances and its one exit for lymphocytes?
cards.back: Entrances: afferent lymph from tissue and HEVs from blood. Exit: the efferent lymphatic, leaving at the hilum.
cards.quote: Think of the node as a hotel with two entrances, afferent lymph from tissue and HEVs from blood, and one exit, the efferent lymphatic.
cards.section: A node samples lymph and blood; the spleen samples blood alone

cards.front: In a resting lymph node, what two observations show that the blood entrance (HEVs) is much busier than afferent lymph?
cards.back: Afferent lymph has only about 5 to 10 percent of the cell concentration of efferent lymph, and, in large-animal cannulation studies, more than 90 percent of efferent-lymph lymphocytes entered through HEVs.
cards.quote: more than 90 percent of the lymphocytes in efferent lymph of resting nodes had entered through HEVs
cards.section: A node samples lymph and blood; the spleen samples blood alone

cards.front: A bacterial antigen enters the bloodstream directly, with no tissue site. Which secondary lymphoid organ is placed to sample it first, and why not a lymph node?
cards.back: The spleen. It filters arterial blood, which brings antigen and lymphocytes; it has no afferent lymphatics and no HEVs. Nodes sample lymph draining tissue.
cards.quote: The spleen, the largest secondary lymphoid organ, has no afferent lymphatics and no HEVs, so it samples blood, not lymph.
cards.section: A node samples lymph and blood; the spleen samples blood alone

cards.front: In a peripheral lymph node HEV, {{c1::L-selectin (CD62L)}} on the lymphocyte binds sulfated mucin-like glycoproteins, tethering the cell and setting it rolling.
cards.back: Step 1 of entry: tether and roll. No signal is needed before it binds.
cards.quote: L-selectin (CD62L) on the lymphocyte binds sulfated mucin-like glycoproteins on the HEV, which tethers a fast-moving cell and sets it rolling.
cards.section: The way in: three steps at the high endothelial venule

cards.front: Which chemokines switch LFA-1 on at a lymph node HEV, and which receptor serves CCL21 and CCL19?
cards.back: CCL21, CCL19 or CXCL13; CCR7 is the receptor for CCL21 and CCL19.
cards.quote: The integrin LFA-1 stays in a low-affinity shape until a chemokine (CCL21, CCL19 or CXCL13) signals through its receptor
cards.section: The way in: three steps at the high endothelial venule

cards.front: L-selectin is already sticky. Why does a lymphocyte at an HEV also need LFA-1, which grips only after a chemokine signal?
cards.back: L-selectin catches and lets go, so the cell rolls but cannot stop. Needing a chemokine first makes the cell commit to stopping only on the HEVs of a lymphoid organ.
cards.quote: Requiring a chemokine signal before the firm grip means the cell commits to stopping only where that signal is presented
cards.section: The way in: three steps at the high endothelial venule

cards.front: A lymphocyte's CCR7 is blocked, but its L-selectin works. Predict its behaviour in a mouse lymph node HEV.
cards.back: It tethers and rolls but would not arrest on the CCL21/CCL19 signal. Without CCR7 signalling LFA-1 is not switched on by those chemokines, so it stays low-affinity and does not bind ICAM-1 and ICAM-2 (CXCL13 aside).
cards.quote: The signal changes LFA-1's shape so it binds ICAM-1 and ICAM-2 on the endothelium, and the cell stops, then crosses the wall.
cards.section: The way in: three steps at the high endothelial venule

cards.front: Mice lacking L-selectin were studied in 1994. What did they show, and what does it say about L-selectin?
cards.back: A severe reduction in lymphocytes in their peripheral nodes, so L-selectin is needed for homing into peripheral nodes.
cards.quote: In 1994 mice lacking L-selectin had a severe reduction in lymphocytes in their peripheral nodes.
cards.section: How the entry molecules were found

cards.front: Besides L-selectin and LFA-1, what adhesion pair do HEVs of the gut's Peyer's patches use?
cards.back: The integrin alpha4beta7 on the lymphocyte binding MAdCAM-1 on the venule.
cards.quote: the integrin alpha4beta7 on the lymphocyte binds MAdCAM-1 on the venule
cards.section: Other routes in

cards.front: Sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) is {{c1::high in blood and lymph and low inside lymphoid tissue}}, and lymphocytes sense it through the receptor S1P1.
cards.back: S1P1 is a G protein-coupled receptor; the gradient guides exit.
cards.quote: The lipid sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) is high in blood and lymph and low inside lymphoid tissue
cards.section: The way out: S1P1 reads the S1P in lymph

cards.front: To test whether lymphocytes need S1P1 to leave lymphoid organs, why did Cyster's group make irradiated mice reconstituted with S1P1-deficient fetal liver cells instead of using whole-body knockouts?
cards.back: Mice lacking S1P1 in every cell do not survive embryonic development; the chimera removes S1P1 only from blood-forming cells.
cards.quote: Mice lacking S1P1 in every cell do not survive embryonic development, so they gave irradiated mice blood-forming cells from S1P1-deficient fetal liver.
cards.section: The way out: S1P1 reads the S1P in lymph

cards.front: S1P1-deficient T and B cells are transferred into normal mice and cannot leave lymphoid organs. What does this transfer add to the chimera result?
cards.back: It places the requirement in the lymphocyte, not its surroundings: the host's S1P and tissues are normal, yet the cells stay trapped.
cards.quote: S1P1-deficient T and B cells transferred into normal mice could not leave lymphoid organs, so the requirement lies in the lymphocyte, not its surroundings.
cards.section: The way out: S1P1 reads the S1P in lymph

cards.front: How does CD69 close the exit gate of an activated lymphocyte?
cards.back: CD69, which appears early after activation, binds S1P1 and opposes its function; the pair is internalized and degraded, so the cell stays in the node.
cards.quote: CD69, a surface protein that appears early after activation, binds S1P1 and opposes its function
cards.section: The way out: S1P1 reads the S1P in lymph

cards.front: What does it mean that lymphocyte exit from the rat spleen is first-order?
cards.back: The same fraction of cells present leaves each minute (about 0.7%), not the same number, whether the spleen holds a thousand cells or a billion.
cards.quote: the same fraction of the cells present leaves each minute, not the same number
cards.section: Why a cell's stay is set by the way out

cards.front: Made-up case: lymphocytes leave an organ by a single first-order step with exit rate constant 0.02 per min. What is the mean residence time?
cards.back: Mean stay = 1 / k = 1 / 0.02 per min = 50 min.
cards.why: For one first-order exit step, the average stay is 1 / the exit rate constant.
cards.quote: the average stay is 1 / that rate

cards.front: Does doubling the rate at which lymphocytes arrive in an organ change how long each one stays there? Why?
cards.back: No. The stay is set only by the exit rate constant; arrival rate changes how many are held, not each cell's stay.
cards.quote: how fast cells arrive has no effect on how long any one of them stays
cards.section: Why a cell's stay is set by the way out

cards.front: Made-up case: 500 naive CD4 and 500 naive CD8 T cells enter one mouse node per hour. CD4 cells stay about 12.2 h and CD8 cells about 21.2 h. How many of each does the node hold at steady state, and what is the CD8:CD4 ratio?
cards.back: CD4: 500 × 12.2 = 6,100. CD8: 500 × 21.2 = 10,600. Ratio 21.2 / 12.2 ≈ 1.74; with equal entry the ratio is the stay alone.
cards.quote: In mice, naive CD4 T cells cross a node in about 12.2 h and naive CD8 T cells in about 21.2 h.
cards.section: Why a cell's stay is set by the way out

cards.front: In the rat model, the spleen receives about twice as many lymphocytes per minute from blood as the subcutaneous nodes, but each cell stays about a quarter as long (2.4 h versus about 10 h). How does the spleen's steady-state holding compare?
cards.back: Holding = entry × stay: 2 × 1/4 = 1/2. The spleen holds about half as many. Traffic alone does not tell you what an organ holds.
cards.quote: Twice the entry times a quarter of the stay gives about half the holding.
cards.section: Why a cell's stay is set by the way out

cards.front: A drug strips S1P1 from a patient's lymphocytes; HEV entry is untouched. Predict the blood lymphocyte count and lymph node size.
cards.back: Blood count falls steeply; nodes gain only a little. Exit is shut, so stays in lymphoid tissue lengthen and the extra cells come out of blood, a small part of the pool.
cards.quote: the blood lymphocyte count falls steeply. The nodes gain only a little, because blood was a small part of the pool to begin with.
cards.section: Why a cell's stay is set by the way out

cards.front: How does fingolimod, a multiple sclerosis drug, lower blood lymphocyte counts?
cards.back: It removes S1P1 from lymphocytes, so the cells are held in lymphoid tissue, not killed.
cards.quote: the cells are held in lymphoid tissue, not killed.
cards.section: Why a cell's stay is set by the way out

cards.front: A lymph node drains a site of immune challenge. Which traffic changes make it enlarge?
cards.back: Migrating dendritic cells arrive in afferent lymph, more lymphocytes enter through HEVs, and for a time fewer leave because, in mouse studies, CD69 removes S1P1 from their surface.
cards.quote: More lymphocytes enter from blood through the HEVs, and for a time fewer leave
cards.section: A draining node holds on to its visitors

cards.front: A draining lymph node comes to hold twice as many lymphocytes as before. Give two different traffic changes that could produce this, and say what would tell them apart.
cards.back: Double the entry with the same stay, or halve the exit rate constant with the same entry (or a mix). Only measuring entry and exit separately can tell which happened.
cards.quote: Double the entry (each cell staying as long as before), or halve the exit rate constant
cards.section: A draining node holds on to its visitors

cards.front: Made-up case: labelled naive T cells enter one of hundreds of peripheral lymph nodes at 400 per hour and each stays 10 h. The node's exit rate constant is then halved, entry unchanged. How many labelled cells does the node hold at the new steady state?
cards.back: Before: 400 × 10 = 4,000. Halving k doubles the stay to 20 h, so 400 × 20 = 8,000 cells.
cards.why: Entry stays fixed because one node is a small part of the pool.
cards.quote: halving exit doubles both the stay and the number held
cards.section: A draining node holds on to its visitors

cards.front: Halving exit from one node out of hundreds doubles the cells it holds. Predict whether halving exit from every node at once doubles each node's holding, and explain.
cards.back: No, it rises much less. The pool is closed: shared longer stays drain blood, and entry into each node falls with the blood count, so holding rises far less than the stay.
cards.why: Rests on holding = entry × stay, with entry proportional to cells in blood.
cards.quote: Then blood is drained, entry into each node falls with it, and the holding rises by much less than the stay
cards.section: A draining node holds on to its visitors

cards.front: What is the immunological benefit of a draining node's transient shutdown of lymphocyte exit?
cards.back: The longer stay gives the rare lymphocytes that recognise the antigen more time to find it. Exit resumes afterwards.
cards.quote: The longer stay gives the rare cells that recognise the antigen more time to find it.
cards.section: A draining node holds on to its visitors

cards.front: Made-up data: a lymph node holds 10,000 photoconverted normal T cells at time zero and 3,700 at 12 h, with no new arrivals counted. Assuming first-order exit, estimate k and the mean residence time.
cards.quote: for first-order exit, cells remaining in the node = N0 x exp(-k t).
cards.section: Design problem (extension)

cards.front: In a made-up node-residence experiment, 10,000 S1P1-deficient T cells fall only to 9,100 over 24 h, while normal cells fall to 1,400. Interpret both results and state one limit.
cards.back: Normal: k ≈ 0.083 per h, mean stay ≈ 12 h. S1P1-deficient: k ≈ 0.004 per h, roughly 250 h, so exit is nearly abolished. Limit: the small loss could be cell death, and S1P1 being needed does not mean it alone sets residence.
cards.quote: For S1P1-deficient cells, ln(10,000 / 9,100) = 0.094 over 24 h, about 0.004 per h, or roughly 250 h
cards.section: Design problem (extension)

cards.front: Designing a test of whether S1P1 sets naive T cell residence in a lymph node: why co-inject normal and S1P1-deficient cells into one normal host, and why photoconvert cells in one node?
cards.back: A single shared host means differences cannot come from the host. Photoconversion marks the cohort inside the node red; later arrivals stay green, so new entry does not blur the measured exit.
cards.quote: Inject them together by vein into one normal host, so differences cannot come from the host.
cards.section: Design problem (extension)
